title: Quantum key distribution over a 2 km free-space channel with a high secure key rate
authors: Kyungdeuk Park, Dongkyu Kim, Dong-Gil Im, Yonggi Jo, Jisu Kim, Jonguk Choi, Yong Sup Ihn
abstract: Free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) provides crucial advantages, including mobility and deployment flexibility, for securing next-generation communication networks. However, practical free-space implementations face major challenges, such as muilti-photon vulnerabilities, spatial mode mismatch, and atmospheric turbulence-induced beam fluctuations. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate a free-space decoy-state BB84 QKD system operating at a 100 MHz repetition rate with a 2.5 ns pulse width over a 2 km outdoor channel. By employing an active beam-wander correction based on fast-steering mirrors (FSMs) and position sensitive detectors (PSDs) con?figuration, our system achieves a secure key rate of 164.8 kbps under a quantum bit error rate (QBER) of approximately 3.3 %. This demonstration provides a practical framework for deploying high-rate, long-distance free-space quantum communication in realistic turbulence environments.
summary: The authors experimentally demonstrated a high-rate Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) system operating over a 2 km outdoor link. They overcame significant hurdles from atmospheric turbulence and beam wander by integrating an active stabilization system using FSMs and PSDs. This work provides a practical framework, achieving a secure key rate of 164.8 kbps, essential for future mobile quantum networks.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is demonstrating high-rate, long-distance Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) over free-space channels affected by atmospheric turbulence and structural drift.
main_result: The system successfully achieved a secure key rate of 164.8 kbps over a 2 km outdoor channel, proving the viability of high-speed quantum communication in realistic environments.
method: The methodology involves implementing an active beam stabilization system using Fast-Steering Mirrors (FSMs) and Position Sensitive Detectors (PSDs) to counteract atmospheric turbulence and structural misalignment during BB84 QKD transmission.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a free-space decoy-state BB84 QKD link operating outdoors over 2 km, utilizing a 100 MHz multi-channel transmitter source. The receiver incorporates active tracking optics (FSMs/PSDs) coupled with coarse alignment via a hexapod platform.
key_observables: Secure key rate (164.8 kbps), Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER $\approx 3.3\%$), and the standard deviation of the secure key rate.
important_parameters: 2 km channel distance, 100 MHz repetition rate, $7.5 \mu	ext{rad}$ pointing resolution requirement, and a closed-loop control bandwidth $>500$ Hz.
main_assumptions: The performance scaling up to 30 km is simulated assuming clear atmospheric conditions; the use of weak coherent pulses necessitates the decoy-state protocol.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic setups, measured spectra, temporal pulse profiles, and critically, show the comparison of coupling efficiency with and without active FSM-PSD feedback loops.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup (transmitter/receiver), describes the necessity and implementation of multi-stage active beam stabilization (coarse alignment followed by high-speed tracking), presents performance metrics comparing stabilized vs. unstabilized operation, and concludes with scalability projections.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenges of deploying quantum communication outside controlled laboratory settings, which is crucial for realizing global quantum networks that rely on free-space links.

(b) Raw intensity profiles of the 660 nm guide laser captured by the receiver CMOS camera at different time intervals. DM: dichroic mirror, FSM: fast-steering mirror, PD: photo-detector, PSD: position sensitive detector, BS: beam splitter, PBS: polarization beam splitter, QWP: quarter waveplate, HWP: half waveplate, SPCM: single photon counting module.

FIG. 3. Characterization of atmosperic turbulence and stabilization performance. (a) Power spectral density of the beam- wander measured by the position-sensitive detector (PSD1) at the receiver. (b) Normalized cumulative energy of the beam- wander as a function of frequency, showing that 90% of the turbulence energy is concentrated below 60 Hz. (c) Histogram of the single-photon coupling efficiency into the MMF measured over a 1-minute interval, comparing the performance with (blue) and without (red) the active FSM-PSD feedback loop.

FIG. 4. Outdoor QKD experimental results and performance analysis. (a) Photographic overview of the 2 km free-space QKD link established at the Agency for Defense Development. (b) Error correction efficiency f(QBER) as a function of the quantum bit error rate (QBER), comparing the experimental performance of the Winnow and LDPC protocols against the ideal error correction limit. (c) Secret key rate per pulse as a function of atmospheric loss, comparing experimental data point (with and without stabilization) with the theoretical simulation. (d) Secret key rate per pulse as a function of channel distance, showing the projected performance up to 30 km under clear-air conditions.
